questions.question: Earth's four layers are far from equal in size. One of them alone makes up about 84 percent of the planet's volume, far more than the other three put together. Which layer is it?
choices: The mantle
The inner core
The outer core
The crust
questions.context: The mantle reaches from the bottom of the crust down to about 2,900 kilometres, so it is the thickest of Earth's four layers and holds most of the planet's volume. Many people picture the core as the biggest part, but the outer and inner core together hold almost all of the rest, and the thin crust is less than 1 percent.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade layer units teach that the mantle is the thickest layer and makes up most of Earth's volume.

questions.question: Earth's crust is not the same thickness everywhere. Under some places it is several times thicker than under others. Where is the crust usually thinnest?
questions.answer: Under the floor of the open ocean
choices: Under the floor of the open ocean
Under a shallow sea near a coast
Under a range of high mountains
Under the middle of a continent
questions.context: Oceanic crust, under the floor of the open ocean, is usually only 5 to 10 kilometres thick, while the crust of the continents is several times thicker, and thickest of all under high mountains. A shallow sea near a coast often covers the drowned edge of a continent, so the crust beneath it is thick continental crust.
questions.grade_note: That the crust is thicker under the continents and thinner under the oceans is a core 6th-grade fact about Earth's layers.

questions.question: The deepest hole ever drilled was bored into the hard rock of a continent, in the far north of Russia. Drillers worked at it for about 20 years and got a little more than 12 kilometres down before the work stopped. How far into Earth's layers did the hole reach?
choices: Partway through the crust
Just past the crust, into the mantle
About halfway through the mantle
Down to the top of the outer core
questions.context: The continental crust there is about 35 kilometres thick, and the hole got only about a third of the way through it, about 0.2 percent of the way to Earth's centre. No drill has ever reached the mantle, let alone the core.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade layer lessons point out that the deepest holes ever drilled go only partway through the crust, to show how little of Earth people have reached.

questions.question: Under Earth's crust lies the mantle. Its rock is hot, and near the core it is more than 3,000 degrees Celsius. What is most of the mantle's rock like?
questions.answer: Solid, yet it flows very slowly
choices: Solid, yet it flows very slowly
Liquid, like the lava of a volcano
Solid, and it never moves at all
Half melted, like slushy snow
questions.context: Almost all of the mantle is solid rock, but it is so hot that over long ages it creeps along, about 1 to 10 centimetres a year. Only small parts of it are partly melted, so the mantle is not the sea of liquid magma that many people picture.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade layer units teach that the mantle is hot rock that is mostly solid but flows very slowly, against the common belief that it is liquid.

questions.question: Below the mantle lies the outer core, a layer more than 2,000 kilometres thick. What is the outer core made of?
choices: Liquid iron and nickel
Solid iron and nickel
Liquid melted rock
Hot solid rock
questions.context: The outer core is molten metal, about 85 to 90 percent iron, with some nickel and a little of a few lighter elements. It lies far too deep to be the source of a volcano's lava.
questions.grade_note: That the outer core is liquid iron and nickel is a standard 6th-grade fact about Earth's layers.

questions.question: At Earth's surface, iron melts at about 1,500 degrees Celsius. The inner core, at Earth's centre, is mostly iron and is hotter than 5,000 degrees, yet it is solid. What keeps the inner core solid?
questions.answer: The enormous pressure so deep down
choices: The enormous pressure so deep down
The nickel mixed in with the iron
The lack of any air or oxygen
The pull of Earth's magnetic field
questions.context: Pressure rises with depth, and at the centre it is millions of times the pressure of the air. Squeezed that hard, iron needs far more heat to melt than it does at the surface, so the inner core stays solid. Melting needs only heat, not air, and nickel melts at a lower temperature than iron.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade layer units teach that the inner core is solid iron and nickel, kept solid by enormous pressure though it is the hottest part of Earth.

questions.question: The world's deepest mine reaches about 4 kilometres underground. Down there the bare rock is about 60 degrees Celsius, so hot that ice is pumped down to cool the tunnels. Why is the rock so hot?
questions.answer: Heat flows up from deep inside Earth
choices: Heat flows up from deep inside Earth
The Sun's heat soaks down through the ground
Melted rock flows just beneath the mine
Hot water seeps down from the surface
questions.context: Earth's inside is very hot, and its heat flows slowly out toward the surface, so the deeper the rock lies, the warmer it is. The Sun's warmth reaches only the top 20 metres or so of the ground, and there is no melted rock under the mine.
questions.grade_note: That temperature rises with depth inside Earth is 6th-grade content, and a deep, hot mine is the everyday case.

questions.question: Earth's core has two layers. Suppose a probe could survive the trip toward Earth's centre and take the temperature of each layer of the core on the way down. What would it find?
questions.answer: The inner core is the hotter layer
choices: The inner core is the hotter layer
The outer core is the hotter layer
The two layers are equally hot
Both are cooler than the mantle
questions.context: Temperature keeps rising all the way toward Earth's centre, so the inner core is hotter than the outer core around it. It is the hottest of all Earth's layers, about as hot as the surface of the Sun, while the mantle above both is far cooler.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade layer units teach that the inner core is the hottest layer, which corrects the common belief that the liquid outer core must be hotter.

questions.question: Rock deep inside Earth is squeezed far harder than rock at the surface, and the squeeze grows with every kilometre down. What makes the pressure rise with depth?
questions.answer: The weight of all the rock above it
choices: The weight of all the rock above it
Heat from the core pushing outward
Earth's spin squeezing it inward
The pull of the Moon from above
questions.context: Every layer of rock presses down on the rock beneath it, so the deeper the rock, the more weight lies on top of it. Only 5 kilometres down the pressure is already more than a thousand times that of the air, and Earth's spin makes it bulge outward at the equator rather than squeezing it.
questions.grade_note: That pressure rises with depth inside Earth, because of the weight of the rock above, is taught with Earth's layers in 6th grade.

questions.question: When Earth was young, much of it was melted by great heat. During that time a great deal of its iron gathered at the centre and became the core. Why did the iron end up at the centre?
questions.answer: Iron is denser than rock, so it sank
choices: Iron is denser than rock, so it sank
Iron is magnetic, so it was pulled inward
The Sun's heat drove the iron inward
Iron cooled first and hardened in the middle
questions.context: Iron is much denser than rock, so in the melted young Earth it sank toward the centre while the lighter rock rose above it. That is why Earth's layers are sorted by density, with the dense metal core at the centre and the light rock of the crust on top.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade layer lessons explain the order of the layers by density: the densest material, iron, sank to the centre.
